newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine president steps up pressure on c. bank.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine president steps up pressure on c. bank.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma stepped up pressure on the central bank on Thursday, summoning its chief Viktor Yushchenko to a meeting following two days of criticism from the cash-strapped government.
"During the talks the president stressed the importance of the National Bank of Ukraine and government clearly co-ordinating matters," a statement from the presidential press office said.

The three-way meeting between Kuchma, bank chief Viktor Yushchenko and newly-appointed Finance Minister Ihor Mityukov followed two volleys of criticism fired by the prime minister and economy minister this week against the central bank.

Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko broadly hinted the bank should provide direct credits to the government after telling parliament there was insufficient money in the economy, and criticised it for not adopting a trading band.
The statement said parliament's delay in approving the budget, which under Ukrainian law should have been passed by January 1, was making it hard for the government to operate.
One Western analyst said the government was running low on cash with the 1997 budget still not passed and was seeking alternative sources of funds.
The central bank is authorised to provide the government with direct credits, although the practice in past years has sent inflation skyrocketing and the central bank is trying to avoid it now.

But the statement said that after the meeting Yushchenko, whose tight monetary policies have won him a solid reputation with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), said the bank would not allow uncontrolled inflation or a destabilised currency.

"The head of the National Bank of Ukraine argued against the possibility of direct credits," the statement said, adding the bank and Finance Ministry would devise a mutual plan of co-operation in a week.
Viktor Suslov, head of parliament's Budget Committee, said at a news conference on Thursday that parliament would debate the budget soon.

Acceptance of the budget and an accompanying package of tax reforms should pave the way for receipt of a three-year, $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) from the IMF, which suspended payments a year ago when it overshot spending targets.

Economy Minister Yuri Yekhanurov, appointed by Kuchma along with Mityukov after he fired four ministers on February 25, said the government and central bank must form mutual policies, at the same time praising the bank for slowing inflation and stabilising the currency.
Inflation is forecast at about 25 percent this year against 39.7 percent in 1996, and 181 percent in 1995.
The hryvnia firmed on Thursday on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange to 1.8285 from 1.8300, and has been stable since its introduction at 1.76 to the dollar last September.
Late last year Lazarenko had suggested he head a commission to oversee central bank activities, although under Ukrainian law parliament is responsible for appointing the central bank head.
Yushchenko was re-appointed to a four-year term in February.
